questions.q_en: The Battle of Diu in 1509 was significant because:
options_en: It marked the beginning of Mughal rule in India.​
It established Portuguese naval dominance in the Indian Ocean.
It led to the foundation of the British East India Company.​
It resulted in the decline of the Vijayanagara Empire.​
questions.solution_en:
• The Battle of Diu in 1509 was a pivotal naval engagement where the Portuguese defeated a joint fleet of the Zamorin of Calicut, the Sultan of Gujarat, and the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt, establishing Portuguese naval supremacy in the Indian Ocean.​

• Mughal rule began with Babur's victory in the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.​

• The British East India Company was founded in 1600

• The decline of the Vijayanagara Empire occurred after the Battle of Talikota in 1565.

questions.q_en: Which battle in 1757 marked the beginning of British colonial dominance in India?
questions.solution_en:
• The Battle of Plassey in 1757, where the British East India Company defeated the Nawab of Bengal, marked the beginning of British colonial dominance in India.​

• The Battle of Buxar in 1764 further consolidated British power but followed Plassey.​

• The Battle of Wandiwash in 1760 was part of the Carnatic Wars between British and French forces.​

• The First Anglo-Mysore War (1767 - 1769) involved conflicts between the British and the Kingdom of Mysore.​

questions.q_en: The Third Battle of Panipat in 1761 was fought between:
options_en: The British East India Company and the Marathas.​
The Marathas and Ahmad Shah Durrani.​
questions.solution_en:
• Fought on January 14, 1761, between the Marathas under Sadashivrao Bhau and the Afghan forces led by Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani), it resulted in a decisive Afghan victory, weakening Maratha power and marking a turning point in 18th-century Indian politics.

• The battle saw massive casualties (over 100,000 soldiers), triggered by a Maratha supply blockade and internal dissent, halting their northward expansion and paving the way for British dominance in India.

questions.q_en: The Battle of Colachel (1741) was significant because_____________.​
options_en: It marked the end of Portuguese power in India.
It was the first time an Indian kingdom defeated a European power at sea.
It led to the establishment of French colonies in India.
It resulted in the British gaining control over Bengal.
questions.solution_en:
• The Battle of Colachel, fought in 1741, was significant as it marked the first time an Indian kingdom, the Kingdom of Travancore under Maharaja Marthanda Varma, defeated a European colonial power, the Dutch East India Company, at sea.

• Travancore forces achieved a decisive victory, capturing De Lannoy and other Dutch officers, and effectively ending Dutch colonial ambitions in the region.

• Following the battle, a treaty known as the Treaty of Mavelikkara was signed between Travancore and the Dutch, solidifying peace and friendship between the two parties.

questions.q_en: The Treaty of Yandabo (1826) ended which war?
questions.solution_en:
• The Treaty of Yandabo (1826) ended the First Anglo-Burmese War, forcing Burma to cede Assam, Manipur, and other territories to the British.

• Burma agreed to pay a substantial indemnity to the British, totaling ≤1,000,000.

• Burma agreed to accept a British Resident at the court of Ava (the Burmese capital).

• Burma renounced all claims in Assam and Manipur, which became British protectorates.

• It established British dominance in the region and laid the foundation for the eventual annexation of Burma into British India.

questions.q_en: Who was the last ruling Nawab of Awadh when the British annexed it in 1856?
questions.solution_en:
• Wajid Ali Shah was deposed by the British in 1856, leading to the annexation of Awadh under the Doctrine of Lapse.

• Lord Dalhousie, the Governor-General of India, implemented the "Doctrine of Lapse" which allowed the British to annex Indian states if they were deemed to be misgoverned or if the ruler died without a male heir.

• The annexation of Awadh further fueled existing tensions between the British and the locals, eventually leading to the Revolt of 1857, with Awadh being a major epicenter of the rebellion.

questions.q_en: Which treaty forced the British to recognize Nepal's sovereignty?
questions.solution_en:
• The Anglo-Nepalese War (1814-1816) ended with the Treaty of Sugauli (1816), reducing Nepal's territory but recognizing its sovereignty.

• Treaty of Lucknow (1801): Signed between the British East India Company and Nawab Saadat Ali Khan of Awadh, leading to the annexation of Rohilkhand, Gorakhpur, and the Doab region, making Awadh a British subordinate state.

• Treaty of Allahabad (1765): Signed after the Battle of Buxar between the British East India Company and Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II, granting the British Diwani rights (revenue collection) of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa, marking the beginning of British rule in India.

• Treaty of Paris (1763): Signed between Britain and France, ending the Seven Years' War, with France losing most of its territories in India except for Pondicherry, Karaikal, Mahe, and Chandernagore, strengthening British dominance.

questions.q_en: Which was the first major uprising against British rule in India?
questions.solution_en:
• The Vellore Mutiny (1806) was the first major armed uprising against British rule in India, led by Indian sepoys.

• It led by Indian sepoys in the Vellore Fort (Tamil Nadu) due to resentment over new military dress regulations, cultural insensitivity, and British oppression; it was brutally suppressed within a day.

• The Revolt of 1857 was the largest but not the first.

• The Santhal Rebellion (1855-56) was led by tribal communities.

• The Chuar Rebellion (1799) was an armed uprising by the Chuar tribes of Jungle Mahals (present-day West Bengal and Jharkhand) against the British East India Company's excessive land revenue demands and exploitation
